practice.stem: Myocardial oxygen DEMAND is determined primarily by which three factors?
options: Coronary blood flow, diastolic filling time and blood oxygen content
Heart rate, hemoglobin concentration and coronary artery patency
Heart rate, contractility and wall stress (preload and afterload)
Diastolic filling time, contractility and arterial oxygen saturation
practice.rationale: Demand goes up with a faster heart rate, stronger contractions and more wall stress (more preload coming back, higher afterload). Coronary flow, diastolic time and oxygen content are the SUPPLY side; the mixed options swap supply factors in.

practice.stem: Most left ventricular coronary perfusion occurs during which part of the cardiac cycle?
options: Systole, when ventricular squeezing pushes blood into the coronaries
Isovolumetric contraction, just before the aortic valve opens
Diastole, when the ventricle relaxes and the coronaries can fill
Equally in systole and diastole, regardless of the heart rate
practice.rationale: "During systole, there's so much squeezing going on that the flow through the arteries [is] not that great"; diastole is when the myocytes get good flow. That's why a very fast heart rate, which shortens diastole, can compromise coronary perfusion.

practice.stem: Variant (vasospastic) angina is most directly caused by:
options: Transient coronary artery vasospasm, often at rest overnight or early morning
A fixed atherosclerotic narrowing that limits flow when exertion raises demand
Acute plaque disruption with thrombus that reduces flow without necrosis
Complete coronary occlusion that causes full-thickness myocardial necrosis
practice.rationale: Variant angina is "a spasm in the muscles" of the coronary artery, "not secondary to atherosclerotic plaques", and often happens at rest. A fixed narrowing with exertion is stable angina; plaque disruption with thrombus is unstable angina; full-thickness necrosis is a STEMI.

practice.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts myocardial ischemia with myocardial infarction?
options: Ischemia is irreversible myocardial cell death; infarction is low oxygen delivery that can still recover
Ischemia and infarction both mean cell death; infarction simply involves a larger area of myocardium
Ischemia always raises troponin; infarction is diagnosed only when the ECG shows ST-segment elevation
Ischemia is inadequate oxygen delivery and potentially reversible; infarction is irreversible cell death
practice.rationale: Ischemic cells "are struggling and not getting enough oxygen" but aren't dead; infarction is prolonged ischemia causing irreversible myocardial cell death. So angina means ischemia, not necessarily infarction. Troponin rises with cell death (not ischemia alone), and NSTEMI is an infarction without ST elevation.

practice.stem: Nitroglycerin primarily lowers myocardial oxygen demand by:
options: Arteriolar dilation, which lowers afterload with little effect on the veins
Blocking cardiac β₁ receptors, which slows heart rate and contractility
Blocking cardiac L-type calcium channels, which slows conduction through the AV node
Venodilation, which reduces venous return and therefore preload and wall stress
practice.rationale: Nitrates are converted to nitric oxide and are "primarily a venodilator": less venous return means less preload and less demand (plus a little coronary vasodilation). Arteriolar dilation/afterload is amlodipine, β₁ blockade is metoprolol, and AV-node slowing is verapamil/diltiazem.

practice.stem: Why is a daily nitrate-free interval prescribed with long-acting nitrates?
options: To prevent nitrate tolerance, so the drug keeps working when it is needed
To let the vasodilation headache wear off before the client goes to sleep
To prevent the reflex bradycardia that nitrates cause during the night
To let preload rise overnight so the coronary arteries can refill fully
practice.rationale: Continuous exposure causes tolerance: "If someone took it 24 hours a day, it would eventually stop working for them." The free interval is usually at night, "when they're resting and sleeping." Nitrates cause reflex tachycardia, not bradycardia, and the interval isn't about headache or refilling.

practice.stem: Which comparison of the calcium channel blocker groups is correct?
options: Verapamil and diltiazem mainly dilate arterioles; amlodipine slows HR and AV conduction
Amlodipine mainly dilates arterioles; verapamil and diltiazem also slow HR and AV conduction
Amlodipine and verapamil are dihydropyridines; diltiazem is the only non-dihydropyridine
All three act equally on the heart and the vessels; they differ only in their duration of action
practice.rationale: The "-pines" (dihydropyridines, amlodipine) are preferential for the periphery and lower afterload with minimal direct effect on HR or the AV node. Verapamil and diltiazem are "preferential for the heart": "no good way to remember them… you just have to put these together."

practice.stem: Which adverse-effect pairing is correct?
options: Amlodipine: constipation · verapamil: peripheral edema · metoprolol: bradycardia
Amlodipine: bradycardia and AV block · verapamil: flushing · metoprolol: fatigue
Amlodipine: peripheral edema · verapamil: constipation · metoprolol: bradycardia
Amlodipine: peripheral edema · verapamil: reflex tachycardia · metoprolol: headache
practice.rationale: The dihydropyridines dilate vessels, so edema ("usually worrisome, but in this case, it's expected"); verapamil "also likes the calcium channels in the gut", so constipation; beta blockers cause bradycardia. Fatigue is a real metoprolol effect, but B pairs amlodipine with AV block and verapamil with flushing (a dihydropyridine effect). AV block belongs to the non-dihydropyridines, and headache/reflex tachycardia are nitrate effects.

practice.stem: Acute coronary syndrome most commonly begins with which event?
options: Slow enlargement of a stable plaque over years until it fixes a narrowing of the artery lumen
Rupture or erosion of an atherosclerotic plaque, exposing collagen and tissue factor
Coronary vasospasm triggered by cold exposure, smoking or cocaine use at rest
A rise in oxygen demand with exertion beyond what a fixed narrowing can supply
practice.rationale: ACS starts when the plaque disrupts and "the body go[es], okay, I've got to cover this up, it's like ripping off a scab": platelets activate and a thrombus forms. Slow plaque growth with rising demand is stable angina, and vasospasm is variant angina.

practice.stem: What distinguishes unstable angina from NSTEMI?
options: NSTEMI has myocardial cell death with elevated troponin; unstable angina does not
NSTEMI shows persistent ST elevation; unstable angina always has a normal ECG
Unstable angina raises troponin; NSTEMI shows ST depression with normal troponin
Unstable angina is caused by vasospasm; NSTEMI is caused by plaque rupture and clot
practice.rationale: Her rule: "unstable angina, no troponin, no ST elevation. NSTEMI, yes troponin, but no ST elevation." Neither has ST elevation (that's STEMI), and both come from plaque disruption with thrombus; vasospasm is variant angina.

practice.stem: An elevated cardiac troponin indicates:
options: An acute MI by itself, as soon as the level is above the normal range
Whether the MI is a STEMI or an NSTEMI, based on how high the troponin level rises
Infarction only, because myocarditis and heart failure do not raise it
Myocardial injury, but not its cause; it is read with symptoms and the ECG
practice.rationale: Troponin "indicates myocardial injury, but it doesn't independently establish the cause" — myocarditis and even heart failure can raise it. STEMI vs NSTEMI is decided by the ECG, "not by how high the troponin rises."

practice.stem: When it can be performed promptly, the preferred reperfusion treatment for STEMI is:
options: Fibrinolytic therapy for every STEMI client, whether or not PCI is available
A high-intensity statin to stabilize the plaque before any reperfusion attempt
Primary PCI in the cardiac cath lab to mechanically open the affected artery
An anticoagulant infusion alone to dissolve the existing clot over several days
practice.rationale: "Primary PCI is what we prefer to do." Fibrinolytics are only considered when timely PCI isn't available because of their bleeding risk. Statins and anticoagulants are part of STEMI care, but they don't reopen the artery; anticoagulants limit new clot formation.

practice.stem: Two clients have the same coronary blockage. One developed collateral vessels while the narrowing grew slowly. Compared with the other client, this client is most likely to have:
options: A smaller area of infarction, because blood can reach the tissue by another path
A larger infarct, because the collaterals divert blood away from the blocked artery
The same outcome, because collateral vessels cannot carry blood past a blockage
Full protection, even if the artery is suddenly and completely occluded by a clot
practice.rationale: Collaterals are "another pathway" for blood, so "their actual area of infarction… will be smaller than someone who has the same blockage" without them. They usually can't fully compensate for a sudden, complete occlusion.

practice.stem: A client reports chest pressure every time he climbs the stairs to his apartment; it goes away within minutes of sitting down. The best explanation is:
options: Coronary vasospasm; flow drops at rest and is restored as soon as he exerts himself
Plaque rupture with thrombus; each episode is a new acute coronary syndrome
A fixed narrowing; flow is adequate at rest but can't meet demand during exertion
Subendocardial infarction; myocytes die and troponin rises with each episode
practice.rationale: This is stable angina — predictable with exertion and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin: "at rest, there are no symptoms and it is when there is an exertional state that the symptoms arise." Vasospasm typically happens at rest, plaque rupture is unstable angina/ACS, and stable angina causes no cell death.

practice.stem: A client with known stable angina wakes with chest pain that does not go away after resting and taking nitroglycerin. The nurse recognizes this as:
options: Expected stable angina; the long-acting nitrate dose needs to be increased
Variant angina; a beta blocker should be started to prevent the spasm
Collateral circulation forming; an outpatient stress test can be scheduled
Possible unstable angina, part of ACS, which requires urgent evaluation
practice.rationale: New, worsening or rest symptoms that rest and nitro don't relieve point to unstable angina — the plaque "knocking on the door" of the big heart attack, so it's an emergency. Beta blockers are avoided in vasospasm, and this isn't a routine outpatient problem.

practice.stem: A client is being taught about prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin. Which statement shows correct understanding?
options: "If the first dose doesn't work, I take two more doses first and call EMS only if those fail too."
"If the first dose doesn't relieve the pain, I call EMS, then take more as directed while I wait."
"I'll keep doing what I was doing after the tablet, to see whether the pain goes away on its own."
"If the first dose doesn't work, I'll take my long-acting isosorbide mononitrate tablet instead."
practice.rationale: "If you take one dose, and it doesn't go away, you call emergency services", with additional doses as directed while waiting, because the plaque may be going unstable. Rest goes with the nitro ("a combination of rest and nitro"), and the long-acting nitrate is for prevention, not acute relief.

practice.stem: A client taking tadalafil asks why he must never take nitroglycerin with it. The nurse's best explanation:
options: Tadalafil blocks the conversion of nitroglycerin to nitric oxide, so nitro won't work
Both drugs cause vasodilation, so together they can drop blood pressure profoundly
Together they slow the heart and AV conduction and can cause a complete heart block
Tadalafil raises preload, cancelling the effect of the nitrate on oxygen demand
practice.rationale: Nitrates + PDE-5 inhibitors (the "Viagra class") "causes a huge, dangerous drop in blood pressure" because both vasodilate — "this comes up a lot in boards." The danger is additive, not cancelled, and bradycardia/AV block are beta blocker and non-DHP CCB effects.

practice.stem: A client having an MI has a suspected right ventricular infarction. Why should nitrates be used cautiously or avoided?
options: Nitrates raise afterload, which an injured right ventricle cannot pump against
Nitrates slow the heart rate, which an injured right ventricle cannot tolerate
Nitrates increase right ventricular contractility and its oxygen demand
Lowering preload reduces filling of a right ventricle already struggling to pump
practice.rationale: Decreasing preload decreases what reaches the right ventricle; "if that right ventricle is already struggling because a bunch of it has been… killed off", the nitrate makes it worse. Nitrates lower preload (not raise afterload) and cause reflex tachycardia, not bradycardia.

practice.stem: A client with stable angina asks which of his medications lowers his future risk of MI rather than relieving chest pain. The nurse identifies:
options: Sublingual nitroglycerin used as needed
Isosorbide mononitrate taken each morning
A high-intensity statin taken daily
Amlodipine taken to lower afterload
practice.rationale: "The high-intensity statin, that's going to be your long-term one" — preventive therapy addresses atherosclerosis. Nitrates and CCBs are antianginals: they reduce ischemic symptoms but don't treat the underlying cause.

practice.stem: A student says, "A total occlusion is always a STEMI, and a partial one is always an NSTEMI." The best response:
options: Not always; a total occlusion of a small vessel can still be an NSTEMI
Correct; the degree of blockage alone decides between STEMI and NSTEMI
Not always; a partial blockage of any size causes a STEMI if troponin is high
Correct; that is why the troponin level is used to separate STEMI from NSTEMI
practice.rationale: "You could have… a total occlusion of a smaller vessel and still have an NSTEMI. It really comes down to the amount of tissue" affected. STEMI vs NSTEMI is separated by the ECG, not by troponin height.

practice.stem: A client with chest pain has a first ECG without ST elevation and a normal first troponin. Why does the nurse expect serial ECGs and troponins?
options: Normal first results rule out ACS, so repeats are only for documentation
Serial values show the exact time the plaque ruptured for the chart
Repeat troponins are needed to choose the dose of fibrinolytic to give
An evolving MI may not show yet; a later change or rise reveals new injury
practice.rationale: "Just because it's not elevated right now doesn't mean things aren't getting worse" — a client caught early may still be heading toward infarction, and troponin rises then falls, so trending it shows new injury. Fibrinolytics aren't given in NSTE-ACS.

practice.stem: A 74-year-old client with diabetes reports nausea, vomiting, sweating and weakness but no chest pain. Which conclusion is correct?
options: MI is unlikely, because crushing chest pain is required before an MI can be considered
MI is still possible; older adults and clients with diabetes may have little or no chest pain
These symptoms point to stable angina, since they began at rest instead of with exertion
MI is ruled out, because MI symptoms only begin during physical exertion, never at rest
practice.rationale: Some clients — "particularly older adults and patients with diabetes" — have minimal or no chest discomfort; her mom's MI "thought she had the flu… throwing up and sweating and felt weak." MI can occur at rest (she laughed at "MI never occurs at rest"), and stable angina is exertional.

practice.stem: After a large MI, a client becomes hypotensive and develops crackles. The best explanation:
options: Surviving myocardium contracts harder, raising afterload and forcing fluid into the lungs
Ventricular remodeling has already restored contractility, so the findings are from the nitrates
Loss of contractile myocardium lowers stroke volume and output, and blood backs up into the lungs
Troponin released from the dead cells is causing vasodilation and leaking from the capillaries
practice.rationale: Necrotic tissue can't contract, so stroke volume, cardiac output and ejection fraction fall, and the study guide ties that loss to pulmonary congestion (the crackles); extensive damage can lead to heart failure or cardiogenic shock. Remodeling contributes to progressive dysfunction, not recovery, and troponin is a marker of injury, not a cause of symptoms.

practice.stem: A STEMI client's SpO₂ is 96% on room air. A new nurse starts oxygen "because MONA says so." The best response:
options: Oxygen is for hypoxemia; it isn't routinely needed with adequate saturation
Correct; every STEMI client needs oxygen to limit the size of the infarct
Oxygen should be given only after primary PCI has reopened the artery
Oxygen is unsafe in STEMI because it causes coronary artery vasospasm
practice.rationale: MONA is "the old mnemonic"; now oxygen is given if hypoxic, but "if someone's sitting 96%, you don't need to throw oxygen on them." Oxygen isn't tied to PCI timing, and the sources don't call it unsafe — just unnecessary at normal saturation.

practice.stem: The family asks why the team is rushing a STEMI client to the cath lab. Which explanation is accurate?
options: The cells in the area have already died, so the rush is only to prevent a second heart attack
Myocardium reperfused before cells die can recover; the faster flow returns, the more is saved
Reperfusion is urgent mainly to bring the troponin level down before it can rise further
Speed matters only for fibrinolytics; PCI works equally well whenever it is eventually done
practice.rationale: "If we can get some blood back before the cells actually die, then we can save them" — "the faster you can get blood flow restored, the more tissue you are going to save." Ischemic cells aren't all dead yet, and the earlier the better applies to both PCI and fibrinolytics.

practice.stem: Chest pressure at rest × 40 min. ECG: ST depression, no ST elevation. Troponin: elevated and rising on repeat. Classify.
options: Unstable angina
STEMI
NSTEMI
Stable angina
practice.rationale: "Yes troponin, no ST elevation, that would be an NSTEMI." Unstable angina has no troponin rise; STEMI needs persistent ST elevation; stable angina is exertional and relieved by rest.

practice.stem: New chest pain at rest, first episode ever. ECG: T-wave inversion, no ST elevation. Serial troponins: normal. Classify.
options: NSTEMI
STEMI
Variant angina
Unstable angina
practice.rationale: No ST elevation and no troponin rise = unstable angina — new-onset or rest angina from an unstable plaque, still ACS. NSTEMI needs a troponin rise, STEMI needs ST elevation, and variant angina is vasospasm, not plaque disruption.

practice.stem: Chest pressure and diaphoresis. First ECG: persistent ST elevation. Troponin drawn, result pending. Next step?
options: Treat as STEMI and move toward the cath lab for PCI now
Wait for the troponin to decide between UA and NSTEMI
Classify as unstable angina until a troponin rise is seen
Treat as NSTEMI, since infarction isn't confirmed yet
practice.rationale: "If we see ST elevation, we don't care about the rest of it" — the client goes to the cath lab as quickly as possible. Waiting on troponin is the pathway only when there's no ST elevation.

practice.stem: Chest pain. ECG on arrival: no ST elevation. ECG repeated 30 min later: new persistent ST elevation. Classify.
options: NSTEMI, since the first ECG had no ST elevation
STEMI; it is now a reperfusion emergency
Unstable angina until troponin results return
NSTE-ACS; repeat ECGs only confirm the first
practice.rationale: "At any point, if we see that ST segment elevated, that is now a STEMI." That's why ACS clients get serial ECGs — an evolving MI can change after the first tracing.

practice.stem: Known chronic heart failure; no chest pain. ECG unchanged from baseline. Troponin mildly elevated and flat on serial draws. Best interpretation?
options: Myocardial injury is present, but troponin alone doesn't establish an acute MI
Acute NSTEMI, because any troponin elevation without ST elevation is an NSTEMI
Unstable angina, because the ECG shows no ST elevation and there's no chest pain
STEMI-equivalent, because troponin is elevated even though the ECG is unchanged
practice.rationale: Troponin "doesn't independently establish the cause" — heart failure can show "very tiny levels" as struggling cells die off. Acute MI needs an acute rise/fall plus symptoms, ECG findings or other evidence of ischemia.

practice.stem: NSTEMI confirmed. Orders: antiplatelet, anticoagulant, high-intensity statin, fibrinolytic. Which order does the nurse question?
options: The antiplatelet
The anticoagulant
The fibrinolytic
The high-intensity statin
practice.rationale: "We do not give fibrinolytic therapy for unstable angina or an NSTEMI" — clot busters are "super, super dangerous" (bleeding), only worth the risk in a STEMI. Antiplatelets, anticoagulants and a high-intensity statin are standard UA/NSTEMI treatment.

practice.stem: ED: chest pain. Client took sildenafil earlier today. Order: sublingual nitroglycerin PRN. Nurse's action?
options: Give it; the interaction matters only with long-acting nitrates
Give it, then hold the next dose only if heart rate exceeds 100
Give it with metoprolol to blunt any reflex tachycardia it causes
Hold the nitroglycerin and notify the provider of the sildenafil
practice.rationale: Nitrates should "never be given with PDE-5 inhibitors" — the combination causes a huge, dangerous drop in BP, which is why the ED asks "very specifically" about Viagra-type drugs before any nitrate. The rule covers all nitrates, and the danger is hypotension, not heart rate.

practice.stem: Chest pain at 0500 at rest; smoker. Pain resolved; no fixed coronary obstruction. Which order does the nurse question?
options: Amlodipine, a dihydropyridine CCB
Propranolol, a beta blocker
Sublingual nitroglycerin as needed
Smoking cessation counseling
practice.rationale: This is variant angina. "Beta blockers are avoided. They will worsen symptoms" — they may worsen spasm. CCBs prevent the spasm, nitrates relieve acute episodes, and smoking is a trigger.

practice.stem: Stable angina on metoprolol. HR 50, BP 138/84. Provider wants to add a CCB. Which choice is least likely to slow the heart further?
options: Verapamil
Diltiazem
Any CCB, since all CCBs slow the heart equally
Amlodipine
practice.rationale: Amlodipine has minimal direct effect on HR and AV conduction. Verapamil and diltiazem "work similarly to beta blockers" (↓ HR, AV conduction, contractility), and beta blockers and non-DHP CCBs both cause bradycardia.

practice.stem: Large STEMI. BP 84/50, crackles, signs of poor contractility. Orders: antiplatelet, anticoagulant, metoprolol, high-intensity statin. Which order does the nurse question?
options: Metoprolol
The antiplatelet
The anticoagulant
The high-intensity statin
practice.rationale: Beta blockers are for selected, hemodynamically stable clients; if the MI has already impaired contraction, "we give a beta blocker, which decreases contractility, we could make the situation worse." The others target thrombus and atherosclerosis. Slide 13 does list beta blockers for selected clients after MI with reduced EF — that is for a stable client; here the problem is hypotension and acutely poor pumping right now.

practice.stem: STEMI at a hospital with no cath lab; timely PCI is not possible. No bleeding contraindications. Best reperfusion option?
options: An anticoagulant alone, which dissolves the existing clot
Fibrinolytic therapy, since timely PCI is unavailable
Wait for serial troponins to confirm infarction first
Nitroglycerin and metoprolol until PCI is possible
practice.rationale: Fibrinolytics are considered for eligible STEMI clients "when we can't do PCI"; they break down the clot. Anticoagulants only limit new clot formation, troponin doesn't change STEMI management, and anti-ischemic drugs don't restore flow.

clinical.title: Scenario 1 — Cardiology clinic
clinical.setting: New stable angina on metoprolol and SL nitroglycerin · weeks 0–4
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Week 0, 1400 61-year-old client, a building superintendent, reports 3 months of chest "pressure" when he climbs the stairs in his building or shovels snow. It sometimes spreads to his left shoulder and goes away after a few minutes of sitting down. No symptoms at rest. Smokes about half a pack a day. History of hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Left knee replacement 5 years ago. Seasonal allergies each spring. Enjoys gardening on weekends. Vital Signs — T 36.8°C · HR 84 · BP 148/90 · RR 16 · SpO₂ 98% on room air Laboratory Results — Troponin normal · hemoglobin normal · LDL cholesterol elevated Orders — Metoprolol (Toprol-XL) daily · nitroglycerin (Nitrostat) sublingual PRN chest pain · high-intensity statin daily · smoking-cessation counseling · return visit in 4 weeks

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the visit data. Which findings are risk factors the plan should address? Select all that apply.
options: Smokes about half a pack a day
History of hypertension
Left knee replacement 5 years ago
Type 2 diabetes
Seasonal allergies each spring
Gardens on weekends
questions.rationale: Stable angina is a warning sign, so the plan also addresses the cardiovascular risk factors — smoking, hypertension, diabetes and physical activity are the modifiable ones named on the slide. An old knee replacement and seasonal allergies aren't cardiac risk factors, and weekend gardening is physical activity, not a risk.

questions.stem: The client's chest pressure pattern is most consistent with which mechanism?
options: A transient spasm of the coronary artery that cuts off supply, typically while at rest
A ruptured plaque with a clot forming over it that partially blocks the artery at rest
Prolonged ischemia that has already caused death of a section of heart muscle
A fixed narrowing that gives enough flow at rest but not when exertion raises demand
questions.rationale: Stable angina: "fixed narrowing, increased demand exceeds the supply, and the pattern is predictable" — stairs and shoveling (exertion, cold) raise demand, and rest brings demand back down. Spasm at rest is variant angina, plaque rupture with clot is unstable angina (ACS), and cell death is infarction — his troponin is normal.

questions.stem: Before the client leaves, which report would require the most urgent follow-up?
options: "The pressure always goes away within a few minutes once I sit down on the stairs."
"Lately the pressure comes on while I'm sitting and watching TV."
"I notice it more when I shovel snow on cold mornings than in the summer."
"My knee aches on the stairs, which is why I sometimes stop to rest halfway up."
questions.rationale: Chest pain at rest is a change from his predictable pattern — new, worsening or rest symptoms signal unstable angina, which is ACS and "knocking on the door" of the big heart attack. Relief with rest and cold as a trigger fit stable angina, and a sore knee isn't cardiac.

questions.stem: Which statements correctly describe how the ordered therapies help this client? Select all that apply.
options: Metoprolol lowers heart rate and contractility, so the heart needs less oxygen
The slower heart rate lengthens diastole, when most coronary perfusion happens
Sublingual nitroglycerin mainly dilates veins, lowering preload and oxygen demand
The statin works right away to stop an angina episode in progress
Metoprolol is chosen because it relieves coronary artery spasm
Quitting smoking addresses the underlying atherosclerotic risk
questions.rationale: Beta blockers ↓ HR and contractility (↓ demand), and the slower rate prolongs diastole, which can improve coronary perfusion. Nitroglycerin is primarily a venodilator → ↓ venous return → ↓ preload → ↓ demand. The statin is "your long-term one" — it lowers future risk, not today's pain — and beta blockers are avoided in vasospasm rather than used for it.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches the client what to do if chest pressure starts. Place the steps in order.
options: Call emergency services if the pain is not relieved
Stop the activity and sit down to rest
Take additional doses as directed while waiting for help
Take one sublingual nitroglycerin tablet
questions.rationale: "Sit down, relax, take a dose of this. It should go away. If it doesn't, now we go and get emergency services." Rest and nitro go together. After the first dose fails he calls EMS right then — not after the second or third — and takes more doses only as directed while waiting.

questions.stem: Week 4. The client returns. Which statements show he needs more teaching? Select all that apply.
options: "If the metoprolol makes me tired, I'll just stop taking it."
"I sit down before I put a nitroglycerin under my tongue."
"If one tablet doesn't work, I'll take three before I call anyone."
"A headache after the nitroglycerin can happen."
"I check my pulse and blood pressure at home."
"Now that I take a statin, I won't get chest pain anymore."
questions.rationale: Stopping a beta blocker abruptly can cause rebound sympathetic activity that precipitates ischemia. EMS is called when the first dose doesn't relieve the pain. The statin reduces future atherosclerotic risk; it doesn't relieve angina. Resting with nitro, expecting a headache (vasodilation) and monitoring HR and BP are correct.

clinical.title: Scenario 2 — Primary care clinic
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Week 0, 0930 44-year-old client seen after an urgent care visit. For a month she has been woken around 0500 by chest tightness that lasts several minutes and then goes away on its own. She runs three mornings a week with no chest symptoms. Smokes a pack a day; reports using cocaine "a few times" this year. Appendectomy at age 20. Takes a daily multivitamin. Urgent care also started propranolol last week for "racing heart." Vital Signs — T 36.6°C · HR 70 · BP 118/74 · RR 14 · SpO₂ 99% on room air Laboratory Results — Troponin normal × 2 · ECG during an episode at urgent care showed ECG changes that resolved when the pain stopped · coronary angiography: no significant fixed blockage Orders — Amlodipine (Norvasc) daily · nitroglycerin sublingual PRN chest pain · smoking-cessation and substance-use counseling

questions.stem: Which findings are consistent with variant angina? Select all that apply.
options: Chest tightness that wakes her early in the morning
No chest symptoms while running
ECG changes during an episode that resolved
Smokes a pack a day and has used cocaine
Appendectomy at age 20
Takes a daily multivitamin
questions.rationale: Variant angina is coronary vasospasm that "often occurs at rest," particularly overnight or early morning, rather than with exertion — so she can run without symptoms. The spasm "can be severe enough that it can be reflected on an EKG", and smoking and cocaine (vasoconstrictive substances) are triggers. The appendectomy and multivitamin are irrelevant.

questions.stem: The client's episodes are most directly caused by which mechanism?
options: A fixed atherosclerotic narrowing that can't meet demand during exertion
Plaque disruption with a clot that partially and suddenly blocks the artery
Transient coronary artery vasospasm that temporarily cuts oxygen supply
Complete occlusion causing full-thickness death of the ventricular wall
questions.rationale: Variant angina is "not secondary to atherosclerotic plaques… it's a spasm in the muscles" — her angiogram shows no significant fixed blockage and her troponins are normal. A fixed narrowing with exertional pain is stable angina, plaque disruption with clot is unstable angina/ACS, and full-thickness death is a STEMI.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the client's medication list. Which finding is the priority to report to the provider?
options: Amlodipine, because it will block the coronary arteries from dilating
Propranolol, because beta blockers can worsen coronary spasm
Sublingual nitroglycerin, because nitrates don't relieve a vasospasm episode
The daily multivitamin, because it will interfere with how amlodipine works
questions.rationale: Beta blockers are generally avoided in isolated vasospastic angina because they may worsen spasm — "beta blockers are avoided. They will worsen symptoms." Calcium channel blockers prevent the spasm, and nitrates relieve acute episodes through vasodilation. Nothing in the sources links a multivitamin to amlodipine.

questions.stem: The provider confirms the amlodipine. Which information does the nurse plan to include in teaching? Select all that apply.
options: It helps prevent spasm of the coronary arteries
It mainly relaxes arterioles, lowering afterload
It will noticeably slow your heart rate and AV conduction
Mild ankle swelling is an expected effect
Constipation is its signature adverse effect
Headache and flushing can occur
questions.rationale: CCBs "make [coronary vessels] less squeezy" and prevent vasospasm. Amlodipine, a "-pine" dihydropyridine, is preferential for the periphery: arteriolar dilation → ↓ afterload, with minimal direct effect on HR and AV conduction. Its adverse effects are peripheral edema ("usually worrisome, but in this case, it's expected"), headache and flushing. Slowing the heart and constipation belong to verapamil.

questions.stem: Which instruction is most important for the nurse to give this client to reduce future episodes?
options: Stop running in the mornings, since the episodes come from exertion
Take the amlodipine only on the nights she expects an episode to occur
Stop smoking and avoid cocaine, since both can trigger the spasm
Stop the propranolol tonight on her own, without waiting to talk to anyone
questions.rationale: Smoking, cocaine and other vasoconstrictive substances, cold and certain medications are variant-angina triggers. Her episodes aren't exertional, so running isn't the problem, and amlodipine is a daily preventive, not a PRN. Beta blockers shouldn't be stopped abruptly (rebound ischemia), so any change goes through the provider.

questions.stem: Week 6. The client returns. Which finding is expected and does not suggest a problem with her therapy?
options: Heart rate 46 with lightheadedness when she stands up
Chest tightness that did not ease after rest and one nitroglycerin
New chest pressure that now comes on while she is running
Mild swelling around both ankles at the end of the day
questions.rationale: Peripheral edema from a dihydropyridine is expected. Bradycardia with symptoms is a non-dihydropyridine (or beta blocker) effect that needs follow-up, pain not relieved by the first nitro means calling EMS, and new exertional pain is a change in pattern that needs evaluation.

clinical.title: Scenario 3 — Emergency department
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 2200 58-year-old client brought in by his spouse with chest pressure that started at rest about an hour ago. Diaphoretic and nauseated. History of hypertension and stable angina; has sublingual nitroglycerin at home but did not take any tonight. When asked directly, he says he took sildenafil (Viagra) earlier this evening. History of gout. Allergic to penicillin (rash). Wears reading glasses. Vital Signs — T 36.9°C · HR 102 · BP 96/60 · RR 20 · SpO₂ 97% on room air Laboratory Results — 12-lead ECG: no ST elevation · troponin #1 pending · potassium normal Orders — Nitroglycerin 1 tablet sublingual now · serial 12-lead ECGs · serial troponins · oxygen PRN for hypoxemia

questions.stem: Which findings require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Chest pressure that began at rest
Diaphoresis and nausea
Took sildenafil earlier this evening
History of gout
Allergic to penicillin
questions.rationale: Chest pressure at rest with diaphoresis and nausea is a possible ACS — "any chest pain we're going to be concerned about until we know otherwise." The low BP and the sildenafil both matter because nitrates are one of the treatments. Gout and a penicillin allergy don't change tonight's priorities.

questions.stem: The client asks why the nurse cares about his Viagra. The best explanation of the interaction is that:
options: Sildenafil blocks absorption under the tongue, so the nitroglycerin won't work
The combination slows conduction through the AV node and causes complete heart block
Both drugs dilate blood vessels, so together they can cause profound hypotension
The combination thins the blood, so nitroglycerin would raise his bleeding risk
questions.rationale: "Nitrates should never be given with PDE-5 inhibitors" — sildenafil "also causes vasodilation, so getting them both together can be very dangerous": a huge, dangerous drop in BP. The sources don't describe absorption, AV-block or bleeding interactions.

questions.stem: Which action is the nurse's priority regarding the nitroglycerin order?
options: Give the nitroglycerin now, because relieving chest pain comes before the BP
Give half the ordered nitroglycerin and recheck the blood pressure in a few minutes
Give the nitroglycerin with oxygen so the drop in pressure is better tolerated
Hold the nitroglycerin and notify the provider about the sildenafil and low BP
questions.rationale: PDE-5 inhibitor use is a "never combine" — the ED asks "very specifically before they administer a nitrate." He's also already hypotensive, where nitrates are used cautiously or avoided. Pain relief doesn't override profound hypotension, a partial dose isn't safe, and his SpO₂ of 97% gives no reason for oxygen.

questions.stem: The provider asks the nurse to screen every chest-pain client before a nitrate is given. Which findings should the nurse report before giving a nitrate? Select all that apply.
options: Takes tadalafil
BP significantly low
Suspected right ventricular infarction
Heart rate in the 70s
History of seasonal migraines
Takes a daily statin
questions.rationale: Nitrates are never combined with PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil or tadalafil) and are used cautiously or avoided with significant hypotension or suspected RV infarction — lowering preload means less blood returns to a right ventricle that's "already struggling." A normal heart rate, migraine history and a statin aren't listed contraindications.

questions.stem: Day 1, 2230. The first ECG shows no ST elevation and troponin #1 returns normal. The client still has mild pressure. What does the nurse do next?
options: Continue serial ECGs and serial troponins, since this may be an evolving MI
Prepare the client for discharge, since a normal troponin rules out a heart attack
Prepare the client for fibrinolytic therapy to break up the clot before it grows
Stop monitoring the ECG, since a STEMI has now been completely ruled out
questions.rationale: "Just because it's not elevated right now doesn't mean things aren't getting worse" — one early troponin may be normal before infarction shows, so ACS is followed with serial ECGs and serial troponins. Fibrinolytics are only for STEMI, and ST elevation can still develop later.

questions.stem: Day 1, 2400. The client is moved to the observation unit. Which findings need follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Troponin #2 is elevated
Dizzy when he sits up; BP 88/54
Chest pressure has resolved
SpO₂ 98% on room air
Spouse asks if he can take his Viagra again next weekend
Asks for a blanket because the room is cold
questions.rationale: A rising troponin without ST elevation now points to an NSTEMI. Symptomatic hypotension needs reporting. The spouse's question is a teaching need — nitrates and PDE-5 inhibitors must never be combined, and his provider has to address it before discharge. Resolved pain and a normal SpO₂ are reassuring; feeling cold is irrelevant.

clinical.title: Scenario 4 — Emergency department
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 0600 66-year-old client with known stable angina. Over the past 2 days her chest pressure has come on with less and less activity, and this morning it woke her from sleep. She sat up, took one sublingual nitroglycerin, and when it didn't help she called EMS and took a second tablet as directed while waiting. Osteoarthritis of both hands. Cataract surgery last year. Lives with her daughter. Vital Signs — T 36.7°C · HR 88 · BP 138/84 · RR 18 · SpO₂ 97% on room air Laboratory Results — 12-lead ECG: ST depression, no ST elevation · troponin #1 normal · hemoglobin normal Orders — Serial 12-lead ECGs · serial troponins · antiplatelet medication · anticoagulant · nitroglycerin · high-intensity statin · cardiology consult for possible coronary angiography

questions.stem: Which findings show that the client's angina is no longer stable? Select all that apply.
options: Chest pressure is coming on with less activity
Chest pressure woke her from sleep
Pain not relieved by rest and one nitroglycerin
Osteoarthritis of both hands
Cataract surgery last year
SpO₂ 97% on room air
questions.rationale: Unstable angina may be new-onset angina, worsening of previously stable angina, or angina at rest (if the client "just wakes up with chest pain"). Stable angina is relieved by rest or nitro — "if they don't relieve the symptoms… we're looking at this as possibly unstable angina." Arthritis, old cataract surgery and a normal SpO₂ are irrelevant.

questions.stem: Which process best explains the change in the client's symptoms?
options: A larger fixed plaque that has grown slowly and now limits flow during exertion
Coronary spasm that occurs at rest without any underlying atherosclerotic plaque
Complete occlusion with full-thickness necrosis of the left ventricular wall
Plaque disruption with a clot that reduces flow, without detectable necrosis yet
questions.rationale: Unstable angina usually results from acute plaque disruption and thrombus — "it's like ripping off a scab" and the body covers it with clot — reducing flow enough for ischemia but not detectable necrosis. Slow fixed growth is stable angina, spasm without plaque is variant angina, and full-thickness necrosis is a STEMI.

questions.stem: The client's daughter says, "Her heart blood test was normal, so why is everyone in such a hurry?" Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "A normal test means it's stable angina, so we are mostly being careful today."
"The plaque is unstable and clotting, and it can soon progress to a heart attack."
"The test result is wrong, because a normal level doesn't happen with chest pain."
"We are hurrying because she needs clot-busting medicine as soon as possible."
questions.rationale: Unstable angina is part of ACS and a medical emergency — "knocking on the door" of the big heart attack, "a pre-warning that things are about to go pretty bad." No troponin rise is exactly what defines UA (it isn't lab error), and fibrinolytics are not given for UA or NSTEMI.

questions.stem: Which therapies does the nurse anticipate for this client? Select all that apply.
options: Antiplatelet medication to reduce platelet-mediated clot formation
Anticoagulant to limit ongoing clot formation and propagation
Fibrinolytic therapy to dissolve the clot
High-intensity statin to stabilize the plaque
Nitroglycerin to reduce myocardial oxygen demand
A calcium channel blocker to treat coronary vasospasm
questions.rationale: UA/NSTEMI treatment: antiplatelets, anticoagulants, anti-ischemic therapy (nitroglycerin, selected beta blockers), a high-intensity statin ("it actually helps to stabilize that plaque") and angiography/PCI when indicated. Fibrinolytic therapy is NOT indicated — "super, super dangerous," reserved for STEMI. Her problem is plaque and clot, not spasm.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks how this client's diagnosis is being sorted out. Place the steps of the chest-pain admission pathway in order.
options: Classify as unstable angina if troponin does not rise
Treat the chest pain as a possible acute coronary syndrome
With no ST elevation, check troponin and repeat it serially
Obtain a 12-lead ECG
questions.rationale: Chest pain → working diagnosis of ACS → ECG first, "because that is fast." ST elevation means STEMI and the cath lab; without it, look at troponin, repeated serially. No ST elevation and no troponin rise = unstable angina; no ST elevation with a troponin rise = NSTEMI.

questions.stem: Day 1, 1400. The client is pain-free on the cardiac unit. Which new finding would change her diagnosis to NSTEMI?
options: The ST depression on her ECG persists on the next serial tracing
A later troponin rises while the ECG still shows no ST elevation
Her next 12-lead ECG shows new, persistent ST-segment elevation
Her chest pressure returns briefly and is relieved by nitroglycerin
questions.rationale: "Yes troponin, no ST elevation, that would be an NSTEMI." ST depression can occur in UA, so it doesn't change the diagnosis, and persistent ST elevation would make it a STEMI — straight to the cath lab. Recurrent pain needs reporting, but it doesn't define NSTEMI.

clinical.title: Scenario 5 — Medical-surgical unit
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 3, 0300 78-year-old client with type 2 diabetes, admitted 3 days ago for cellulitis of the left lower leg. Calls for help: "I just feel weak and tired, like I'm coming down with the flu." Vomited once; skin is sweaty. Denies chest pain or pressure. Cellulitis redness is receding inside the marked border. Wears bilateral hearing aids. Her daughter is staying overnight. Vital Signs — T 37.0°C · HR 98 · BP 132/80 · RR 22 · SpO₂ 96% on room air Laboratory Results — Fingerstick glucose within her usual range · 12-lead ECG: T-wave inversion, no ST elevation · troponin #1 elevated Orders — Repeat troponin and ECG · notify cardiology · continue IV antibiotic

questions.stem: Which findings at 0300 require follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: New weakness and fatigue
Vomited once
Sweaty skin
Cellulitis redness receding
Wears bilateral hearing aids
Glucose within her usual range
questions.rationale: MI symptoms vary: dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, dizziness or unusual fatigue can be the presentation — the instructor's mom "thought she had the flu… throwing up and sweating and felt weak." Receding redness shows the cellulitis is improving, and hearing aids and a usual glucose are irrelevant.

questions.stem: The daughter says, "She can't be having a heart attack — she has no chest pain." Which explanation is accurate?
options: Older adults and people with diabetes may have minimal or no chest discomfort
A heart attack is ruled out until the chest pain begins, so we are watching closely
Her antibiotic is masking chest pain, which will appear once the infusion ends
Atypical symptoms like hers mostly occur in younger men, so this is unusual for her
questions.rationale: Some clients have minimal or no chest discomfort, particularly older adults and people with diabetes and women more often report nausea, dyspnea or fatigue. No chest pain doesn't exclude MI. The sources don't say antibiotics mask pain, and atypical presentations aren't a young-male pattern.

questions.stem: Day 3, 0600. Troponin #2 is higher than #1, and the repeat ECG still shows no ST elevation. The client is most likely experiencing:
options: Non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI)
Unstable angina with ischemia but no cell death
ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)
Stable angina triggered by the stress of her infection
questions.rationale: Rising troponin = myocardial cell death; no ST elevation = not a STEMI. "Yes troponin, no ST elevation, that would be an NSTEMI." Unstable angina has no troponin rise, and stable angina doesn't cause necrosis.

questions.stem: Cardiology confirms an NSTEMI. Which items does the nurse anticipate in the plan? Select all that apply.
options: Antiplatelet medication
Anticoagulant
Fibrinolytic (clot-busting) therapy
High-intensity statin
Oxygen by nasal cannula for her SpO₂ of 96%
Coronary angiography if indicated by her risk and findings
questions.rationale: UA/NSTEMI: antiplatelet, anticoagulant, anti-ischemic therapy, high-intensity statin, and angiography/PCI when indicated. Fibrinolytics are not indicated for UA or NSTEMI — "when it's a smaller heart attack, it is usually not worth the risk." Oxygen is for hypoxemia: "if someone's sitting 96%, you don't need to throw oxygen on them."

questions.stem: Day 4, 0800. Troponin is now lower than yesterday's peak. Which nursing action is appropriate?
options: Stop the troponin draws, since a falling value means the MI is fully over
Restart the troponin series only if she develops classic crushing chest pain
Continue trending the troponin and report any new rise or new symptoms
Request a fibrinolytic in case the troponin begins to rise again tomorrow
questions.rationale: Troponin rises and then falls, and "we will keep trending it down… then if [the client] does have another set of symptoms, we can go, hey… starting back to rise. Then we know that something new" is happening. Waiting for classic chest pain is risky in a client who presents atypically, and fibrinolytics aren't used in NSTEMI.

questions.stem: Day 5. The nurse reviews warning signs with the daughter before discharge. Which statements show correct understanding? Select all that apply.
options: "Mom may not get chest pain, so nausea, sweating or unusual tiredness count too."
"They kept checking her troponin so they could spot any new damage."
"Her ECG never showed ST elevation, so it wasn't a real heart attack."
"Women may have nausea, shortness of breath or fatigue with a heart attack."
"A high troponin by itself proves exactly what caused the damage."
"Clot-busting drugs are the usual treatment for her type of heart attack."
questions.rationale: Atypical symptoms are common in older adults, people with diabetes and women, and serial troponins catch a new rise. An NSTEMI is a real MI — the ECG separates STEMI from NSTEMI, not whether necrosis happened. Troponin shows injury, not its cause, and fibrinolytics aren't used for NSTEMI.

clinical.title: Scenario 6 — Emergency department → cath lab
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 0815 54-year-old client arrives by EMS with crushing chest pressure that began at rest after breakfast, radiating to his jaw and left arm. Diaphoretic and anxious. Smokes; told last year his cholesterol was high. Hernia repair 10 years ago. Bowls in a weekly league. No recent surgery, bleeding or stroke. Vital Signs — T 36.8°C · HR 96 · BP 142/88 · RR 20 · SpO₂ 96% on room air Laboratory Results — 12-lead ECG: ST elevation · troponin #1 pending Orders — Activate cath lab for primary PCI · antiplatelet medication · anticoagulant · nitroglycerin sublingual PRN chest pain if BP permits · high-intensity statin · oxygen PRN for hypoxemia

questions.stem: Which findings require immediate action? Select all that apply.
options: Crushing chest pressure at rest radiating to the jaw and left arm
ST elevation on the 12-lead ECG
Diaphoresis
SpO₂ 96% on room air
Hernia repair 10 years ago
Bowls in a weekly league
questions.rationale: Persistent chest pressure at rest with radiation and diaphoresis is a classic MI presentation, and ST elevation makes it a STEMI. An SpO₂ of 96% doesn't need treatment, and an old hernia repair and bowling are irrelevant.

questions.stem: The ECG and symptoms are most consistent with which condition?
options: STEMI — an acute occlusion causing infarction, often through the full wall depth
NSTEMI — infarction confirmed by an elevated troponin, with no ST elevation
Unstable angina — a clot reducing flow with no myocardial cell death
Stable angina — pain from exertion against a fixed plaque, relieved by rest
questions.rationale: ST elevation = STEMI: "either big enough… or more commonly… it's the entire wall depth." NSTEMI has no persistent ST elevation, unstable angina has no ST elevation and no troponin rise, and stable angina is exertional and relieved by rest.

questions.stem: Troponin #1 is still pending. What is the priority?
options: Wait for the troponin result to confirm infarction before activating the cath lab
Repeat the 12-lead ECG in a few hours to see whether the ST elevation persists
Get the client to the cath lab for PCI without waiting for the troponin
Give fibrinolytic therapy first, even though the cath lab here is available
questions.rationale: "If we see ST elevation, we don't care about the rest of it" — the client goes to the cath lab as quickly as possible. Primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy when it can be done promptly; fibrinolytics are for eligible clients when timely PCI isn't available. Reperfusion saves ischemic myocardium before irreversible cell death, so waiting costs muscle.

questions.stem: While the cath lab team is on the way, which therapies does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
options: Antiplatelet medication to reduce platelet aggregation
Anticoagulant to limit additional clot formation
Nitroglycerin for ischemic pain if the BP permits
High-intensity statin
Oxygen for every client with chest pain, whatever the SpO₂
Amlodipine to prevent coronary vasospasm
questions.rationale: STEMI treatment: restore flow (PCI), prevent further thrombus (antiplatelets, anticoagulants), reduce demand (nitroglycerin when BP permits, selected beta blockers), and reduce future events (high-intensity statin). Oxygen is "for hypoxemia, not routinely" — the old MONA habit. Vasospasm isn't this client's problem.

questions.stem: Day 1, 0840. The client's BP drops to 88/52 and the provider suspects right ventricular involvement. While awaiting transport to the cath lab, the client asks for another nitroglycerin. What does the nurse do?
options: Hold the nitroglycerin and report the low BP and suspected RV infarction
Give the nitroglycerin, since relieving his ischemic pain lowers oxygen demand
Give the nitroglycerin and add a beta blocker to bring down his heart rate
Give the nitroglycerin and lay him flat to protect his blood pressure afterward
questions.rationale: Nitrates are used cautiously or avoided with significant hypotension or suspected RV infarction — less preload means less blood to a right ventricle that's already struggling. STEMI nitroglycerin is "when blood pressure and clinical circumstances permit," and beta blockers are only for selected, hemodynamically stable clients.

questions.stem: Day 1, 1100. The client returns from PCI. Which findings indicate the treatment is working? Select all that apply.
options: Chest pressure has resolved
No new rise in troponin on serial draws
New irregular rhythm on the monitor
Breathing comfortably with SpO₂ 97% on room air
BP 84/50 with new crackles in both lungs
Asks when he can return to his bowling league
questions.rationale: Restoring flow relieves ischemia; serial troponins are trended so a new rise would flag new injury — no new rise is reassuring. Comfortable breathing on room air shows no oxygen need. A new dysrhythmia (electrical instability) and hypotension with crackles (failing pump) are MI complications that need follow-up. The bowling question is irrelevant to whether reperfusion worked.

clinical.title: Scenario 7 — Cardiac care unit
clinical.setting: Large anterior MI and its consequences · days 2–6
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 2, 0700 69-year-old client admitted 2 days ago with a large STEMI treated with PCI. Overnight he became short of breath lying flat; crackles in both lung bases this morning. The monitor shows short runs of an irregular rhythm. Former smoker who quit 5 years ago. Enjoys crossword puzzles; his wife visits every afternoon. Vital Signs — T 37.1°C · HR 112 · BP 92/58 · RR 24 · SpO₂ 91% on room air Laboratory Results — Troponin elevated, trending down from yesterday's peak · echocardiogram: reduced ejection fraction Orders — Metoprolol daily (due 0900) · antiplatelet medication · high-intensity statin · oxygen PRN for hypoxemia · cardiac rehabilitation referral

questions.stem: Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Crackles in both lung bases
BP 92/58 with cool, clammy skin
Short runs of an irregular rhythm
Troponin trending down from yesterday's peak
Reduced ejection fraction
Enjoys crossword puzzles
questions.rationale: Crackles, hypotension, dysrhythmias and a reduced EF are consequences of losing functioning myocardium. Troponin rising and then falling is the expected pattern after an MI — follow-up would be needed if it started to rise again. Crosswords are irrelevant.

questions.stem: The runs of irregular rhythm are best explained by which consequence of MI?
options: Rebound sympathetic activity from stopping his beta blocker too abruptly
Coronary vasospasm triggered by the catheters used during his recent PCI procedure
Nitrate tolerance developing from receiving nitroglycerin around the clock
Ischemic, injured tissue disrupting normal impulse formation and conduction
questions.rationale: Electrical instability: "ischemia and injured tissue can disrupt normal impulse formation and conduction, producing dysrhythmias" — "to make the situation even more fun on top of dealing with the heart attack." He hasn't stopped a beta blocker, and spasm and nitrate tolerance don't explain a post-MI dysrhythmia here.

questions.stem: Based on his findings, the client is most likely experiencing:
options: A new infarction, shown by a troponin that is still elevated two days after PCI
A failing pump — the damaged LV ejects less, so output falls and blood backs into the lungs
An expected recovery from PCI that needs only routine vital signs and no report
Profound hypotension caused by a nitrate taken together with a PDE-5 inhibitor
questions.rationale: Necrotic myocardium can't contract well → ↓ SV and CO (hypotension) and the study guide links lost contractile myocardium to pulmonary congestion (crackles, dyspnea). A large infarct can lead to heart failure or cardiogenic shock. His troponin is falling, not rising, and nothing suggests a PDE-5 inhibitor.

questions.stem: The nurse plans ongoing monitoring. Which consequences of this client's MI should the nurse watch for? Select all that apply.
options: Dysrhythmias
Progressive heart failure from ventricular remodeling
Cardiogenic shock
Rebound hypertension from his statin
Peripheral edema caused by his antiplatelet medication
Worsening pulmonary congestion
questions.rationale: Consequences of MI: loss of contractile tissue, ↓ SV/CO and EF, electrical instability, ventricular remodeling leading to heart failure, and — when damage is extensive — cardiogenic shock; LV backup causes pulmonary congestion. The statin and antiplatelet effects listed aren't in the sources (peripheral edema is an amlodipine effect).

questions.stem: Day 2, 0900. Metoprolol is due. BP is 94/60 and crackles persist. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Give the metoprolol, because slowing the heart rate will lower his oxygen demand
Give the metoprolol and recheck his blood pressure after the dose takes effect
Hold the metoprolol and notify the provider of his hypotension and poor contractility
Hold the metoprolol and teach him he must never take a beta blocker again
questions.rationale: Beta blockers are for selected, hemodynamically stable clients: if the MI is large enough to impair contraction and "we give a beta blocker, which decreases contractility, we could make the situation worse." Lowering demand is the goal only in a milder MI. Holding a dose and reporting differs from banning the class forever. Slide 13 does list beta blockers for selected clients after MI with reduced EF — that is for a stable client; here the problem is hypotension and acutely poor pumping right now.

questions.stem: Day 6. The client is stable and preparing for discharge. Which statements show he understands his long-term plan? Select all that apply.
options: "The statin helps stabilize my plaque and lowers my future risk."
"I'll stay off cigarettes for good."
"If the metoprolol makes me tired, I'll stop it on my own."
"The antiplatelet medicine helps keep new clots from forming."
"My artery is open now, so my risk factors don't matter."
"Nitroglycerin will reverse my plaque if I take it every day."
questions.rationale: High-intensity statins and risk-factor management address the underlying atherosclerosis; antiplatelets reduce platelet aggregation and new thrombus. Stopping a beta blocker abruptly risks rebound ischemia. PCI opens one artery but doesn't remove his risk, and nitrates relieve symptoms — "no single medication addresses every problem."

clinical.title: Scenario 8 — Rapid rounds
clinical.setting: Clinic, ED and inpatient · one question each
clinical.text: Five clients, one question each. Read each stem on its own.

questions.stem: A client with a STEMI arrives at a hospital where timely PCI is not available, and the provider is considering fibrinolytic therapy. Which finding in the client's history should the nurse report before it is given?
options: Had abdominal surgery two weeks ago
Smoked a pack a day for 30 years
Takes amlodipine for blood pressure
SpO₂ is 97% on room air
questions.rationale: The danger of fibrinolytics is bleeding — "you're basically breaking down every single clot in the body," so a client who "had surgery two weeks ago… can't get it"; the biggest risk is intracranial bleeding. Smoking, amlodipine and a normal SpO₂ don't affect eligibility in the sources.

questions.stem: A client's troponin returns elevated. Which conditions can cause an elevated troponin? Select all that apply.
options: Myocardial infarction
Myocarditis
Heart failure
Stable angina relieved by rest
Unstable angina
questions.rationale: Troponin indicates myocardial injury but doesn't establish the cause: myocarditis kills off some cardiac cells, and heart failure can show "very tiny levels" as a struggling heart's cells slowly die. Stable angina is reversible ischemia without cell death, and unstable angina by definition has no troponin rise.

questions.stem: A client with chronic stable angina takes verapamil. Which findings should the nurse report or address? Select all that apply.
options: Heart rate 46
No bowel movement in 4 days
Dizziness with BP 86/52
Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day
Chest pain relieved after resting
questions.rationale: Non-dihydropyridines act on the heart: bradycardia, AV block and hypotension — and verapamil "also likes the calcium channels in the gut," causing constipation. Peripheral edema is the dihydropyridine (amlodipine) effect, and chest pain relieved by rest fits his stable angina.

questions.stem: A client taking isosorbide mononitrate (Imdur) every morning asks why it isn't taken around the clock. Which response is correct?
options: "Taking it overnight would cause rebound angina when you wake up in the morning."
"A nitrate-free time each day, usually at night, prevents tolerance to the drug."
"Nitrates only work during exercise, so a dose overnight would simply be wasted."
"Taking it around the clock would make your ankles swell from fluid build-up."
questions.rationale: Repeated or continuous exposure produces nitrate tolerance, so long-acting regimens need a daily nitrate-free interval — usually at night, "because hopefully at night they're resting and sleeping." "If someone took it 24 hours a day, it would eventually stop working." Rebound ischemia is a beta-blocker warning, and ankle edema belongs to amlodipine.

questions.stem: A client with stable angina tells the nurse, "I ran out of my metoprolol 3 days ago, but I feel fine." What is the nurse's main concern?
options: Without metoprolol, the client's coronary arteries will develop vasospasm
Stopping metoprolol can cause hypotension and bradycardia over the next day
Missing metoprolol leads to tolerance, so it must be restarted at a lower dose
Rebound sympathetic activity after abrupt withdrawal can precipitate ischemia
questions.rationale: Avoid abrupt discontinuation of a beta blocker because rebound sympathetic activity may precipitate ischemia ("rebound ischemia with abrupt withdrawal"). Bradycardia and hypotension are effects of taking it, not stopping it; tolerance is a nitrate problem, and vasospasm isn't caused by stopping it.

cards.back: Oxygen supply is insufficient to meet myocardial oxygen demand

cards.front: Three main determinants of myocardial O₂ demand
cards.back: Heart rate · contractility · wall stress (preload + afterload)

cards.front: Three determinants of myocardial O₂ supply
cards.back: Coronary blood flow · diastolic filling time · O₂ content of blood (Hgb + O₂ sat)

cards.front: When does most left-ventricular coronary perfusion occur?
cards.back: Diastole — during systole there's so much squeezing that flow through the coronaries is poor

cards.front: Why can a very fast heart rate cause ischemia?
cards.back: ↑ HR raises O₂ demand and shortens diastolic filling time → less coronary perfusion

cards.front: How does collateral circulation protect myocardium?
cards.back: Gives another pathway for blood around the blockage → smaller infarct than the same blockage without collaterals
Ischemia = inadequate O₂ delivery, potentially reversible · Infarction = prolonged ischemia → irreversible cell death. Angina = ischemia, not infarction
Chest pressure, squeezing, heaviness · radiates to arm (especially left), shoulder, jaw, neck, back · may have dyspnea, nausea, diaphoresis
Fixed atherosclerotic narrowing; flow OK at rest but can't keep up when demand rises → reversible ischemia, no cell death
Physical exertion · emotional stress · cold exposure · heavy meals
Transient coronary artery vasospasm, not a fixed plaque. Not common, but "still in the NCLEX test plan"

cards.front: When does variant angina typically occur?
cards.back: At rest — especially overnight or early morning

cards.front: Variant angina: drug of choice and drug to avoid
cards.back: CCBs prevent the spasm ("less squeezy"); nitrates relieve acute episodes; beta blockers are avoided — they worsen spasm

cards.front: Unstable angina — why is it an emergency?
cards.back: Plaque has become unstable with clotting starting — it's "knocking on the door" of the big heart attack; part of ACS
New-onset angina · worsening of previously stable angina · angina at rest
NBC — "if you remember the network": Nitrates, Beta blockers, Calcium channel blockers
SL nitroglycerin (Nitrostat) for an acute attack · isosorbide mononitrate (Imdur) long-acting to prevent episodes
Converted to nitric oxide → mainly venodilation → ↓ venous return → ↓ preload → ↓ wall stress → ↓ O₂ demand

cards.front: SL nitro teaching: chest pain not relieved after first dose?
cards.back: Call EMS after the first dose fails; may take 2nd/3rd doses as directed while waiting. Sit down and rest with it
Headache (vasodilation) · hypotension and dizziness · reflex tachycardia
Never combine — both vasodilate → profound hypotension. "This comes up a lot in boards"; the ED asks about Viagra-type drugs before any nitrate

cards.front: Why prescribe a daily nitrate-free interval?
cards.back: Prevents nitrate tolerance — usually at night, when they're resting and sleeping; taken 24 h/day it would stop working

cards.front: Beta blocker prototype and antianginal mechanism
cards.back: Metoprolol — block β₁ → ↓ HR and ↓ contractility → ↓ O₂ demand

cards.front: Why avoid abruptly stopping a beta blocker?
cards.back: Rebound sympathetic activity may precipitate ischemia
Bradycardia · hypotension · fatigue · AV conduction abnormalities — monitor HR and BP
Dilates arterioles → ↓ afterload; minimal effect on HR/AV node. "-pine" = periphery
Prefer the heart: ↓ HR, ↓ AV conduction, ↓ contractility (like a beta blocker) + some vasodilation. "No good way to remember them — just put these two together"
Peripheral edema (also headache, flushing) — "usually worrisome, but in this case, it's expected"
Bradycardia, AV block, hypotension — they slow conduction through the AV node
Constipation — verapamil also likes the gut's calcium channels → weaker peristalsis

cards.front: Stable angina long-term plan: two goals
cards.back: 1) Relieve ischemic symptoms (NBC) · 2) Reduce cardiovascular risk (statin, antiplatelet, ACEI/ARB, risk factors)

cards.front: Which therapy lowers future atherosclerotic risk rather than relieving angina?
cards.back: High-intensity statin — the long-term one; SL nitro and vasodilators are the immediate ones

cards.front: Modifiable risk factors to address in stable angina
cards.back: Smoking · hypertension · diabetes · physical activity — antianginals treat symptoms, prevention treats the cause

cards.front: Why aren't antianginals a substitute for preventive therapy?
cards.back: They only reduce symptoms; preventive therapies address atherosclerosis, thrombosis risk and long-term outcomes
Plaque rupture or erosion — "like ripping off a scab"; the body covers it with clot
Unstable angina · NSTEMI (non-ST-elevation MI) · STEMI (ST-elevation MI)
No troponin, no ST elevation — reduced flow but no myocardial cell death
"Yes troponin, no ST elevation" — myocardial cell death has occurred
Yes troponin, yes ST elevation — usually full (transmural) wall depth has died

cards.front: What primarily distinguishes STEMI from NSTEMI?
cards.back: The ECG (ST elevation) — not how high the troponin rises
Location — the left anterior descending (LAD) artery; probably a STEMI, but a small LAD branch could give an NSTEMI. Amount of tissue supplied decides damage
ECG — fast; leads on the chest right away

cards.front: ECG shows ST elevation — next step?
cards.back: STEMI — "if we see ST elevation, we don't care about the rest of it": straight to the cath lab (fibrinolytics if no cath lab)

cards.front: No ST elevation: how do you tell NSTEMI from unstable angina?
cards.back: Troponin — rise/fall = NSTEMI; stays normal on serial checks = unstable angina

cards.front: Why serial ECGs and troponins in ACS?
cards.back: It may be an evolving MI — one normal reading early doesn't rule it out; trending also catches a new injury

cards.front: Therapy NOT indicated for unstable angina/NSTEMI
cards.back: Fibrinolytics (clot busters) — too risky; only for STEMI
Antiplatelet · anticoagulant · anti-ischemic (nitro, selected BBs) · high-intensity statin · angiography/PCI when indicated

cards.front: Ischemia vs infarction at the cell level
cards.back: Ischemia: ↓ ATP, ↓ contraction, electrical instability — can recover if reperfused · Infarction: necrosis, troponin released

cards.front: Who may have an MI with little or no chest pain?
cards.back: Older adults and patients with diabetes; women more often report nausea, dyspnea, fatigue
Felt like the flu: vomiting, sweating, weak, no chest pain — no crushing chest pain doesn't exclude MI

cards.front: Troponin — what is it and why is it in blood?
cards.back: A contractile protein inside cardiac cells; released into blood when myocardial cells are injured/die

cards.front: Does elevated troponin alone prove MI?
cards.back: No — shows myocardial injury, not the cause (e.g., myocarditis, heart failure); MI = troponin + symptoms + ECG

cards.front: Consequences of losing functioning myocardium after MI
cards.back: ↓ contractility → ↓ SV and CO · ↓ EF · dysrhythmias · ventricular remodeling → heart failure (or cardiogenic shock if extensive)
Primary PCI (cardiac cath lab) when it can be done promptly

cards.front: When are fibrinolytics considered for STEMI?
cards.back: Eligible STEMI patient when timely PCI is not available
Bleeding — breaks down every clot in the body; worst risk is intracranial bleed; many contraindications (e.g., recent surgery)
Save ischemic myocardium before irreversible cell death — the faster flow returns, the more tissue saved
Antiplatelets ↓ platelet aggregation; anticoagulants limit ongoing clot formation/propagation

Only in hemodynamically stable patients — ↓ contractility can worsen a heart already pumping poorly after a big MI (long-term, selected post-MI clients with reduced EF can benefit once stable — slide 13)
Only if hypoxemic — MONA (morphine, O₂, nitrates, aspirin) is the old mnemonic; "if someone's sitting 96%, you don't need to throw oxygen on them"

qa.q: (student asked) How does overall anemia affect angina?
qa.a: Anemia affects the whole body; with a coronary blockage it definitely makes ischemia worse, but long before it kills myocytes the patient would be too short of breath to get out of bed — no direct cause-and-effect with angina.

qa.q: (student asked) How long does sublingual nitroglycerin take to help?
qa.a: "Five minutes, I believe" — and the patient should be resting, not continuing the activity: rest + nitro together.

qa.q: (student asked) What is the washout time between a PDE-5 inhibitor and a nitrate?
qa.a: She wasn't sure of the exact washout time; the ED asks very specifically about Viagra-type drugs before giving any nitrate, because a client can take one and show up hours later with an MI.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which change increases myocardial oxygen demand?
qa.a: Answer not read aloud (Kahoot froze). From slide 4: demand rises with ↑ heart rate, ↑ contractility and ↑ wall stress (preload/afterload).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Coronary perfusion occurs mostly during…?
qa.a: Diastole — so a very fast heart rate shortens diastolic filling time and can compromise coronary perfusion.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Stable angina most often occurs because of…?
qa.a: "That one was pretty easy" — a fixed atherosclerotic narrowing; demand rises (exertion) and supply can't keep up (from slide 9). The Kahoot then froze.

qa.q: (student asked) Is the "widow maker" a STEMI?
qa.a: "Widow maker" is about location — the left anterior descending artery. It's probably going to be a STEMI, but a small branch of the LAD could give an NSTEMI: how much heart the artery supplies decides the damage.

qa.q: (student asked) How quickly do troponin results come back?
qa.a: When the lab knows it's urgent it's run very fast — she didn't want to give an exact number ("usually less than five minutes").

qa.q: (student asked) Does troponin rise and then fall?
qa.a: Yes — a rise and then a fall. That's another reason for serial troponins: trend it down, so if it starts rising again you know there's a new injury.

qa.q: (student asked) How does troponin leave the blood?
qa.a: The body clears it naturally (filtered through the kidneys); she wasn't sure of the chemistry.

qa.q: (student asked) What is the danger of fibrinolytic therapy?
qa.a: Bleeding — it breaks down every clot in the body. Many contraindications (e.g., surgery two weeks ago); the biggest risk is intracranial bleeding.

qa.q: (Kahoot) What best describes myocardial ischemia?
qa.a: Oxygen supply is insufficient for myocardial oxygen demand.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Why may collateral circulation protect some myocardium?
qa.a: It gives another pathway for blood to reach the tissue past the blockage.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Variant angina is most directly caused by…?
qa.a: Transient coronary artery vasospasm (answer not read aloud; from slide 10).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Nitroglycerin primarily lowers oxygen demand by…?
qa.a: Primarily venodilation → ↓ venous return → ↓ preload; it also does a little coronary artery vasodilation.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which nitrate combination can cause profound hypotension?
qa.a: "Right, good" — nitrate + sildenafil (Viagra): both vasodilate, so together they're very dangerous.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Why is a nitrate-free interval sometimes prescribed?
qa.a: To prevent nitrate tolerance (answer not read aloud; from slide 12 + 00:15:17).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Metoprolol reduces angina mainly by…?
qa.a: ↓ heart rate and ↓ contractility → ↓ oxygen demand — she expected the class to know beta blockers well by now.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which drug primarily reduces afterload with little direct AV-node effect?
qa.a: Amlodipine — "the -pines" are the dihydropyridines, preferential for the periphery; verapamil and diltiazem prefer the heart.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which adverse effect is especially associated with verapamil/diltiazem?
qa.a: Bradycardia / AV block — they slow conduction through the AV node and lower heart rate.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which class is especially useful for preventing coronary vasospasm?
qa.a: Calcium channel blockers (answer not read aloud; from slide 10).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which treatment mainly lowers future atherosclerotic risk rather than immediately relieving angina?
qa.a: High-intensity statin — the long-term one; sublingual nitroglycerin and coronary vasodilators are the immediate ones.

qa.q: (Kahoot) ACS commonly begins with which event?
qa.a: Plaque rupture or erosion (answer not read aloud; from slide 19).

qa.q: (Kahoot) What distinguishes unstable angina from NSTEMI?
qa.a: Myocardial necrosis shown by troponin: NSTEMI has an elevated troponin, unstable angina doesn't (answer not read aloud; from slide 20).

qa.q: (Kahoot) A patient has ischemic symptoms and elevated troponin without persistent ST elevation. This is most consistent with…?
qa.a: "Good, yes troponin, no ST elevation, that would be an NSTEMI."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which finding is characteristic of a STEMI?
qa.a: Persistent ST-segment elevation (answer not read aloud; from slide 20).

qa.q: When we actually have a STEMI, what are we going to do? How are we going to get some blood back?
qa.a: Restore coronary blood flow ASAP — the cardiac cath lab for PCI; fibrinolytics if PCI isn't possible (her answer at 00:53:59).

qa.q: (student asked) During PCI, how do they know where to go?
qa.a: They inject dye (angiogram) and can see where blood should be flowing and isn't; then a balloon pushes the vessel open and a stent keeps it open.

qa.q: (student asked) Would troponin still be elevated a month after an MI?
qa.a: It sticks around for a while — she thought about 14 days to clear completely (not sure). In her mom's case troponin didn't show it, but the ECG changes did.

qa.q: (student asked) Femoral or radial access for the cath?
qa.a: Femoral is traditional: client lies flat at least 6 hours, can't bend at the waist, higher risk of bleeding and clotting. Radial is smaller and harder but has fewer risks; for a STEMI they more often go femoral because radial takes longer.

qa.q: (student asked) What is recovery from CABG like?
qa.a: A sternotomy — "cracking it in half" — is a big, intense recovery: chest tubes and lines; prepare clients for that.

qa.q: (student asked) What if the blockage is very large?
qa.a: The balloon may not inflate or go in; stents come in different lengths; with many bad blockages stenting may only buy time. Medication released locally prevents clotting at the stent, and afterwards the client needs antiplatelet medication.

qa.q: (Kahoot) What is the purpose of anticoagulant therapy in acute coronary syndrome?
qa.a: To limit ongoing clot formation and propagation (answer not read aloud; from slide 42).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which therapy is not indicated for unstable angina and NSTEMI?
qa.a: "Very good" — fibrinolytic therapy: clot busters are super dangerous with lots of risks, so they're only for STEMIs.

qa.q: (Kahoot) If ischemic myocardium is reperfused before irreversible injury, it may…?
qa.a: "Good" — recover: get blood back before the cells die and you save them.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which statement about MI symptoms is most accurate?
qa.a: Some clients — especially older adults and people with diabetes — have minimal or no chest discomfort. She laughed at the distractor "MI never occurs at rest."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Does an elevated troponin level by itself establish the cause?
qa.a: No — it shows that something is injuring myocardium, not what; it's read with symptoms and the ECG (slide 34).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Why are serial troponin measurements useful?
qa.a: They identify an acute rise or fall that signals new injury (answer not read aloud; from slide 34).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Loss of functioning myocardium after MI can cause…?
qa.a: ↓ contractility → ↓ stroke volume and cardiac output, ↓ EF, dysrhythmias, heart failure or cardiogenic shock (answer not read aloud; from slide 35).

qa.q: (Kahoot) When promptly available, the preferred STEMI reperfusion method is…?
qa.a: "Primary PCI is what we prefer to do."

qa.q: (Kahoot) When may fibrinolytic therapy be considered?
qa.a: For an eligible STEMI client when timely PCI isn't available (answer not read aloud; from slide 37).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Why is rapid reperfusion important in STEMI?
qa.a: To save ischemic myocardium before irreversible cell death — the faster flow is restored, the more tissue saved (slide 37 + 00:59:08).
